title: React Hooks Handbook: State, Effects & the Rules That Govern Them
summary: A dense, example-driven field guide to React hooks — how useState really schedules updates, how useEffect dependencies and cleanup actually work, the rules of hooks and why they exist, and how to factor logic into custom hooks. Covers internals, practical patterns, comparisons, and the mistakes that bite most often.

chapters.title: What Hooks Are & Why They Exist
points: Definition: a hook is a plain function starting with `use` that lets a function component tap into React features (state, lifecycle, context) between render calls.
Pre-hooks pain: stateful logic could only live in class components; reuse required HOCs and render props, producing 'wrapper hell' in the component tree.
Classes also split one concern across three lifecycles (`componentDidMount`, `componentDidUpdate`, `componentWillUnmount`) while unrelated concerns got merged into the same method.
Hooks reorganize code by concern, not by lifecycle phase: one subscription's setup and teardown sit in one `useEffect`.
Hooks shipped in React 16.8 (Feb 2019); they are 100% backward compatible — no rewrite of classes required, both can coexist.
The core built-ins: `useState`, `useEffect`, `useContext`, `useReducer`, `useMemo`, `useCallback`, `useRef`.
Hooks do NOT work inside class components, and `this` is irrelevant in hook code — a common source of confusion when porting.
Mental model shift: a component is a function that runs top-to-bottom on every render; hooks give that function a memory that survives between runs.
Example: `function Counter(){ const [n,setN]=useState(0); return <button onClick={()=>setN(n+1)}>{n}</button> }` — 4 lines replace a class with constructor and bind.
Hooks are opt-in per component; you can migrate one component at a time.

chapters.title: useState: The Basics
points: Signature: `const [state, setState] = useState(initialValue)` — returns a two-element array, destructured by convention.
The initial value is used ONLY on the first render of that component instance; later renders ignore the argument entirely.
Lazy initialization: pass a function, `useState(() => expensiveCompute())`, so the work runs once instead of every render.
Gotcha: `useState(expensiveCompute())` still CALLS the function every render and throws the result away — the parens are the bug.
Setter identity is stable across renders; React guarantees the same `setState` reference, so it is safe to omit from dependency arrays.
Calling the setter with the same value (compared by `Object.is`) lets React bail out and skip re-rendering that subtree.
Multiple independent state slices are idiomatic: `const [name,setName]=useState(''); const [age,setAge]=useState(0);` rather than one object.
State is per-component-instance: rendering `<Counter/>` twice gives two fully independent counters.
A state update is a request, not an assignment — `state` in the current render's scope never changes after the setter runs.
Example of that: `setN(n+1); console.log(n)` logs the OLD value, because `n` is a `const` captured by this render.

chapters.title: State Updates: Batching, Queues & the Functional Form
points: Functional updater: `setN(prev => prev + 1)` reads the latest queued value instead of the render-time closure value.
Classic bug: `setN(n+1); setN(n+1)` increments by 1 total; `setN(p=>p+1); setN(p=>p+1)` increments by 2.
React batches multiple setState calls in one event handler into a single re-render — one paint, not one per call.
React 18 introduced automatic batching everywhere: promises, `setTimeout`, and native event handlers batch too; React 17 only batched inside React event handlers.
`flushSync(() => setN(1))` from `react-dom` opts out of batching when you must read the DOM immediately after — use sparingly, it hurts performance.
Update queue mechanics: each setter call pushes an update onto a queue; at render time React replays the queue over the base state to compute the next value.
Rule of thumb: use the functional form whenever the next state derives from the previous state, or when the setter runs inside an async callback or effect.
State must be treated as immutable — `state.items.push(x); setItems(state.items)` mutates the same array reference, `Object.is` sees no change, and no re-render happens.
Correct object update: `setUser(u => ({...u, age: u.age + 1}))`; correct array append: `setItems(i => [...i, newItem])`.
Spread is shallow — nested updates need nesting: `setState(s => ({...s, addr: {...s.addr, city}}))`.
Derived values do NOT belong in state: compute `const total = items.reduce(...)` during render instead of syncing a second state variable.

chapters.title: Under the Hood: How React Remembers Hook State
points: Each component instance (fiber) holds a singly-linked list of hook objects, stored on the fiber's `memoizedState` field.
There is no key or name attached to a hook — React identifies each hook purely by its CALL ORDER within the render.
On mount React walks the list appending a node per hook call; on update it walks the same list in the same order and reads node N for the Nth call.
This positional identity is the entire reason the rules of hooks exist: a conditional hook shifts every later hook's index by one.
Simplified model: `let hooks = []; let i = 0;` — `useState` does `hooks[i] ??= initial; return [hooks[i], v => {hooks[i]=v; rerender()}]` with `i++` per call.
Each hook node stores its own memoized value, an update queue, and a pointer to the next hook.
State values live on the fiber, not in the closure — that's why they survive re-renders even though local variables do not.
Every render creates a brand-new closure: new props, new state constants, new function objects. Old closures still exist and still see old values.
The 'stale closure' family of bugs all trace back to this: an old callback captured render #1's variables and is still being invoked at render #10.
Dispatchers: React swaps the internal hook implementation between mount and update phases, which is how it throws 'Invalid hook call' when called outside a render.

chapters.title: Rules of Hooks
points: Rule 1 — only call hooks at the top level: never inside conditionals, loops, nested functions, or after an early `return`.
Rule 2 — only call hooks from React function components or from other custom hooks; not from plain utility functions or class methods.
Why: hook state is matched by call index, so a skipped or extra call misaligns every subsequent hook on that component.
Broken: `if (isLoggedIn) { useState(0) }` — on the render where the flag flips, the next hook reads the wrong slot.
Fixed pattern: hoist the hook out and make the CONDITION part of the value — `const [x,setX]=useState(0); const shown = isLoggedIn ? x : null;`.
Early-return trap: any `if (!data) return <Spinner/>` must sit BELOW every hook call in the function body.
Loops: don't `items.map(() => useState())`; extract a child component and give each item its own instance.
Custom hooks are exempt from rule 2 as callees — a `useX` may call other hooks because it is inlined into the caller's hook list.
The `use` naming prefix is not cosmetic: `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` uses it to decide which functions get rule enforcement.
Enable `react-hooks/rules-of-hooks` (error) and `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` (warn); the linter catches nearly all violations statically.
'Invalid hook call' at runtime usually means one of: broken rules, mismatched React and ReactDOM versions, or two copies of React in node_modules.
React 19's `use()` API is the deliberate exception — it CAN be called conditionally, unlike every other hook.

chapters.title: useEffect: Purpose & Timing
points: Signature: `useEffect(setupFn, deps?)` — the setup function runs AFTER React commits the render to the DOM and the browser paints.
Effects are for synchronizing with systems outside React: network requests, subscriptions, timers, DOM APIs, logging, non-React widgets.
Effects are not lifecycle callbacks. The right question is 'what external thing does this render need to stay in sync with?', not 'when does this fire?'.
The setup function must return either nothing or a cleanup function — returning anything else is an error, which is why `useEffect(async () => {})` is illegal (async returns a Promise).
Async pattern: define and call inside — `useEffect(() => { const run = async () => {...}; run(); }, [])`.
`useLayoutEffect` runs synchronously after DOM mutation but BEFORE paint — use only to measure layout or prevent a visible flicker; it blocks painting.
Ordering per commit: React updates DOM → browser paints → effects flush (`useEffect`), versus DOM updates → layout effects flush → paint (`useLayoutEffect`).
In React 18 StrictMode dev builds, every effect is deliberately mounted, unmounted, and remounted once to surface missing cleanup — this does not happen in production.
Don't use an effect to transform data for rendering — compute it during render. Don't use one to handle a user event — put that in the event handler.
Anti-pattern: `useEffect(() => setFullName(first + ' ' + last), [first,last])` causes a second render; just compute `const fullName = first + ' ' + last`.
Effects run per committed render, so an effect that unconditionally sets state it also depends on creates an infinite render loop.

chapters.title: The Dependency Array
points: Three distinct forms: no array (run after every render), `[]` (run once after mount), `[a,b]` (run after mount and whenever `a` or `b` changed).
Comparison is `Object.is` on each slot, positionally — not deep equality. Two structurally identical objects are different deps.
The array length must be constant between renders; React warns 'The final argument passed to useEffect changed size between renders'.
Correctness rule: every reactive value used inside the effect — props, state, context, and values derived from them — must be listed.
`exhaustive-deps` is a correctness lint, not a style preference; suppressing it with `// eslint-disable-next-line` is how stale-closure bugs ship.
Objects, arrays, and functions defined in the component body get a NEW identity every render, so listing them re-runs the effect every render.

Fixes for unstable deps, in preference order: move the value inside the effect; move it outside the component if it's constant; depend on primitive fields (`user.id` not `user`); memoize with `useMemo`/`useCallback` as a last resort.
Refs (`ref.current`) and state setters are stable and need not be listed.
Empty `[]` is a claim that the effect never needs to re-sync — if the effect reads a prop, that claim is a lie and the prop will be permanently stale.
Stale-closure demo: `useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(() => setCount(count+1), 1000); return () => clearInterval(id); }, [])` freezes at 1 — fix with `setCount(c => c + 1)`.
If a dep changes too often, that's a design signal — consider `useReducer` so the effect depends only on the stable `dispatch`.
React Compiler (React 19+) can auto-memoize, reducing manual `useCallback`/`useMemo`, but the dependency rules themselves are unchanged.

chapters.title: Cleanup Functions
points: The function returned from an effect is the cleanup; React calls it before the next run of that same effect and once at unmount.
Full cycle on a dep change: cleanup with OLD values runs first, then setup with NEW values runs.
Cleanup closes over the render that created it, so it always tears down exactly what that render set up — no manual bookkeeping of 'previous' values.
Must-clean resources: `setInterval`/`setTimeout`, `addEventListener`, WebSocket/EventSource connections, external store subscriptions, `IntersectionObserver`/`ResizeObserver`, animation frames.
Timer example: `useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(tick, 1000); return () => clearInterval(id); }, [])`.

Listener example: `useEffect(() => { window.addEventListener('resize', onResize); return () => window.removeEventListener('resize', onResize); }, [onResize])` — same function reference required for removal.
Fetch race condition: two rapid requests can resolve out of order and render stale data.
Ignore-flag fix: `useEffect(() => { let ignore = false; fetch(url).then(r=>r.json()).then(d => { if(!ignore) setData(d) }); return () => { ignore = true } }, [url])`.
Better fix: `AbortController` — `const c = new AbortController(); fetch(url,{signal:c.signal}); return () => c.abort()` — cancels the in-flight request and frees the connection.
Missing cleanup symptoms: memory leaks, duplicated event handlers, timers firing after unmount, and 'setState on unmounted component' warnings.
StrictMode's double-invoke is the free test for this: if your effect breaks when run twice, it lacks proper cleanup.
Some effects genuinely need no cleanup (a one-shot analytics ping) — returning nothing is fine and explicit.

chapters.title: Custom Hooks
points: A custom hook is just a function whose name starts with `use` and which calls other hooks — no special API, no registration.
Purpose: share stateful LOGIC between components. It does not share state — each caller gets its own independent state.
`useToggle`: `function useToggle(init=false){ const [on,setOn]=useState(init); const toggle=useCallback(()=>setOn(o=>!o),[]); return [on,toggle]; }`.
`useLocalStorage`: lazy-init state from `localStorage.getItem`, then write back in an effect keyed on `[key, value]`.
`useDebounce`: `useEffect(() => { const id=setTimeout(()=>setDebounced(value), delay); return ()=>clearTimeout(id); }, [value, delay])`.
`usePrevious`: `const ref=useRef(); useEffect(()=>{ref.current=value}); return ref.current` — returns the value from the previous render.
`useFetch`: bundle `data`/`loading`/`error` state plus an `AbortController` cleanup behind one call site.
Return shape convention: array (`[value, setter]`) when callers will rename freely, object (`{data, loading, error}`) when there are 3+ values.
Custom hooks compose — a hook may call other custom hooks, and its hook calls are inlined into the caller's hook list.
Extract when logic is duplicated across components, when a component body gets long, or when an effect deserves a descriptive name (`useOnlineStatus` beats a bare effect).
Do NOT extract a generic `useMount`/`useEffectOnce` wrapper — it hides deps from the linter and encourages lifecycle thinking.
Custom hooks are testable in isolation with `renderHook` from `@testing-library/react`.

chapters.title: Comparisons & Choosing the Right Tool
points: `useState` vs `useReducer`: `useState` for independent, simple values; `useReducer` when the next state depends on several fields or many actions update the same object.
`useReducer` bonus: `dispatch` is stable, so effects and callbacks can depend on it without re-running.
`useState` vs `useRef`: state re-renders on change and is snapshot-per-render; a ref mutates in place, never triggers a render, and is read as `ref.current`.
Use a ref for values you need to remember but not display: timer IDs, DOM nodes, previous values, instance flags.
`useMemo` vs `useCallback`: `useMemo(fn, deps)` caches the RESULT of calling `fn`; `useCallback(fn, deps)` caches the function itself — `useCallback(f,d) === useMemo(() => f, d)`.
`useEffect` vs `useLayoutEffect`: async after paint vs sync before paint; default to `useEffect` and reach for layout effects only to avoid visual flicker.
`useEffect` vs event handler: if it happens because a user did something, it belongs in the handler; if it must be true for a given render, it belongs in an effect.
Hooks vs class lifecycles: `componentDidMount` ≈ `useEffect(fn, [])`; `componentDidUpdate` ≈ `useEffect(fn, [deps])`; `componentWillUnmount` ≈ the cleanup return.
That mapping is approximate — one effect can span all three phases, and effects run after paint while `componentDidMount` runs before it.

Local state vs context vs external store: lift only as far as needed; `useContext` re-renders every consumer on value change; `useSyncExternalStore` is the correct primitive for external mutable stores.
Prop drilling 2–3 levels is usually cheaper than reaching for context.

chapters.title: Performance & Trade-offs
points: Every state update re-renders that component and, by default, its entire subtree — re-render means running the function, not necessarily touching the DOM.
Reconciliation cost is roughly O(n) in the number of elements rendered; DOM commits are the expensive part, and React skips unchanged nodes.
`useMemo`/`useCallback` are not free: they cost an allocation, a deps array, and a comparison on every render, plus retained memory.
Memoize when the computation is genuinely expensive, when the value is a dep of an effect, or when it's a prop to a `React.memo` child.
`React.memo` on a child is defeated by any inline object, array, or arrow-function prop — a new reference every render fails the shallow compare.
State colocation is the cheapest optimization: push state down to the smallest component that needs it and the re-render radius shrinks.
`children` as a prop lets a stateful parent re-render without re-rendering the passed subtree, since those elements are created by the grandparent.
Too many separate `useState` calls updated together are batched anyway — splitting state does not multiply renders inside one handler.
Effects that set state cause a second render pass before paint completes; a chain of interdependent effects multiplies that cost and usually signals a modeling error.
Measure before optimizing: React DevTools Profiler flamegraph, the 'Highlight updates' setting, and `<Profiler>` callbacks.
React Compiler shifts memoization from manual to automatic, changing the trade-off but not the underlying render model.

chapters.title: Common Mistakes & Gotchas
points: Expecting state to update synchronously: `setCount(1); console.log(count)` logs the previous value — reads happen against this render's snapshot.
Mutating state directly (`arr.push`, `obj.x = 1`) so `Object.is` sees no change and the UI never updates.
Missing deps because the linter warning was disabled — the effect closes over stale props forever.
Object or array literals in the deps array, which are never `Object.is`-equal and re-run the effect every single render.
`useEffect(() => { setData(compute(a)) }, [a, data])` — depending on the state the effect sets creates an infinite loop.
Forgetting cleanup for intervals and listeners, causing leaks and duplicate handlers that compound on every dep change.
`useEffect(async () => {...})` — the returned Promise is mistaken for a cleanup function.
Calling a setter with a value instead of a function inside an interval or async callback, freezing on the first render's value.
Conditional or early-return hook calls that shift hook indices and throw 'Rendered fewer hooks than expected'.
Using `useState` for a value that is never rendered (a timer ID, a mutable flag) — that's what `useRef` is for.
Storing derived data in state and syncing it with an effect instead of computing it during render.
Blaming StrictMode's intentional double-effect for a real missing-cleanup bug, and 'fixing' it with a `didMount` ref guard.
Passing a raw `onClick={handler()}` instead of `onClick={handler}` — the call fires during render and often sets state, looping.

chapters.title: Summary & Quick Reference
points: Hooks give function components memory; that memory is a linked list on the fiber, indexed by call order.
Call hooks only at the top level, only from components or custom hooks — the entire rule follows from positional identity.
`useState`: initial value used once; setter is stable; use the functional updater whenever next state depends on previous.
Treat all state as immutable and replace it with new references; batching means multiple setters in one handler yield one render.
`useEffect` synchronizes with the outside world after paint; it is not a lifecycle hook and not a place to derive render data.
Deps must list every reactive value read inside the effect; comparison is `Object.is`, positional, and shallow.
Return a cleanup for anything that keeps running — timers, listeners, sockets, in-flight requests — and let StrictMode double-invoke prove it.
Custom hooks share logic, not state; name them `use*` and return arrays for pairs, objects for records.
Reach for `useReducer` when many actions touch one state shape, and for `useRef` when a value shouldn't cause renders.
Optimize by colocating state and measuring first; `useMemo`/`useCallback` have real costs and are not defaults.
Turn on `react-hooks/rules-of-hooks` and `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` — most hook bugs in this handbook are caught statically.
Debug checklist for a stale value: which render's closure am I in, what are my deps, and does my cleanup undo my setup?
